intro: Read the deck for the law and the studies and these notes for how to use them. Each note beside a slide explains what to remember and where practitioners slip. Work the section examples, answer the recall questions without looking, and run the ten-question diagnostic on a service you know.

sections.title: What governance means
sections.big_idea: Many field failures are failures of governance: the money is spent but the people paid to deliver are **not answerable to the people they serve**.
in_plain_words: A school with a building and a salaried teacher can still teach little if the teacher does not turn up. The inputs view counts buildings, budgets and posts. The governance view asks who decides, who delivers, who checks and what happens when delivery fails. The World Bank defines governance as the traditions and institutions by which authority is exercised.

The Worldwide Governance Indicators give six composite scores built from perceptions in 35 sources. They help compare countries over long periods but they lag reforms, hide gaps between states and carry margins of error. **Treat a national score as a starting question** and then look at administrative data, audits and field checks.

left.title: Inputs view
items: Cannot explain two districts, one budget

key_terms.meaning: The traditions and institutions by which authority is exercised.
The set of organisations such as ministries, courts and panchayats.
Six composite governance indicators built from perception data.
Adopting the forms of a functional state while function stays absent.
A benefit guaranteed by law, such as the right to information.

worked_example.title: Test a governance score claim
worked_example.setup: A report says 'our state's governance score rose two points, so the school feeding programme is working'. Apply the deck's four cautions.
steps: Perception: the score records what experts and respondents believe, which may reflect news coverage.
Lag: perceptions may trail actual reforms by years, so the rise may not reflect this programme.
Aggregation: a national score hides gaps between states and districts.
Margins of error: a two-point change may sit inside the uncertainty band.
Replace the claim with evidence from the site: administrative data, audits and unannounced visits.
worked_example.answer: The score cannot support a claim about one programme. Use site-level evidence.

mistakes: Treating a large government as proof of strong governance.
Using a national governance score to justify a decision about a single programme site.
Believing a law or agency works because it exists on paper.
Copying the institutions of rich countries and expecting their results.

recall.q: What is the difference between government and governance?
recall.a: Government is the set of organisations. Governance is how those organisations, plus citizens, parties, media and markets, behave together.

recall.q: How many dimensions does the WGI have, and what kind of data feeds them?
recall.a: Six dimensions, built from perception data in 35 cross-country sources.

recall.q: Give two reasons to be careful with governance scores.
recall.a: Any two of: perception, lag, aggregation, margins of error.

recall.q: What is isomorphic mimicry?
recall.a: Adopting the forms of functional states while the function stays absent.

sections.title: The accountability relationship
sections.big_idea: Accountability needs **answerability and enforcement** together, and it runs vertically, horizontally and through citizens' own action.
in_plain_words: Accountability is a relationship in which one party explains its conduct and the other can impose a consequence. Explanation without sanction is public relations, and sanction without explanation is arbitrary. O'Donnell's vertical accountability runs from citizens to rulers, horizontal accountability runs between state agencies, and societal accountability adds citizens' associations and media.

The World Development Report 2004 triangle names four relationships: voice, compact, management and client power. Use it as a diagnostic by asking which relationship broke. **Fixing the wrong relationship wastes the programme's effort**, as the anganwadi example shows.

key_terms.meaning: Information and justification by the powerful to those they serve.
Sanctions or rewards that follow from the explanation.
State agencies checking each other, such as CAG and courts.
Citizens, movements and media pushing agencies into action.
Via politicians and departments, or directly to the provider.

worked_example.title: Which relationship broke?
worked_example.setup: Illustrative, from the deck: a village anganwadi centre is open only two days a week. Test each WDR relationship in turn.
steps: Voice: residents rarely raise it with elected members, so the remedy is a gram sabha agenda item or a women's group petition.
Compact: standards exist but supplementary nutrition funds arrive late, so raise release delays with the district programme officer.
Management: the supervisor post has been vacant for a year, so push to fill it and use the grievance portal.
Client power: mothers have no forum, so start a monthly community meeting where attendance records are read aloud.
worked_example.answer: One failure with four possible breaks. Check all four before choosing a remedy.

mistakes: Treating answerability alone as accountability, with no one able to impose a consequence.
Assuming elections alone hold a service accountable. A vote judges a whole government once in five years.
Reading the Bangladesh absentee figure as current. The deck calls it old.
Using a tool aimed at client power when the compact or management link is the one that broke.

recall.q: What are the two parts of accountability?
recall.a: Answerability and enforcement.

recall.q: Name the four relationships in the WDR 2004 triangle.
recall.a: Voice, compact, management and client power.

recall.q: What is the difference between the long route and the short route?
recall.a: The long route goes citizen to politician to department to provider. The short route is client power directly over the provider.

recall.q: What did O'Donnell conclude about horizontal checks?
recall.a: They depend heavily on vertical ones, because public opinion pushes agencies to act.

sections.title: Principals, agents and absent providers
sections.big_idea: Absence and leakage are **agency problems**, and the three responses are monitoring, incentives and selection, each with costs.
in_plain_words: A principal hires an agent who knows more about their own effort and may have different goals. In government every agent is also a principal, so the chain runs from citizens to legislators, ministries, districts and the frontline, and information is lost at every link. Public agents also face multiple principals, multitasking, hard-to-measure output and weak exit.

Unannounced visits across six countries found 19 percent of teachers and 35 percent of health workers absent, and in India only about half of government primary teachers were teaching. A later study estimated that monitoring is far more cost-effective than hiring. **Diagnose the system before you blame staff**, since duties, travel and unpaid salaries also cause absence.

diagram.caption: a chain of principals and agents

key_terms.meaning: An agent acts for a principal but has private information and different goals.
The principal cannot see the agent's effort.
The agent knows something the principal does not.
Rewarding measured tasks draws effort from unmeasured ones.
A survey counting who is present and working.

worked_example.title: Absence in a school of 20
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: apply the deck's figures to a government primary school with 20 teachers. India's absence rate is 23.6%, and about 1 in 2 teachers were actually teaching on arrival.
steps: Teachers absent: 20 × 0.236 = 4.72, so about 5 on a typical visit.
Teachers actually teaching at the rate of one in two: 20 × 0.5 = 10.
The gap between posts filled and teaching delivered is 20 − 10 = 10 teacher positions.
worked_example.answer: About 5 absent and about 10 teaching out of 20 posts. Presence is only the floor.

mistakes: Using a shame list as the only response, which can breed collusion and false records.
Paying for test scores alone, so teachers neglect non-tested skills.
Reading absence as laziness without checking election duty, travel and unpaid salaries.
Spending on inputs alone in a system with weak management.

recall.q: What are the three standard responses to the principal-agent problem?
recall.a: Monitoring, incentives, and selection and motivation.

recall.q: What did Chaudhury and colleagues find on average in six countries?
recall.a: 19 percent of teachers and 35 percent of health workers absent.

recall.q: What did Muralidharan and colleagues estimate as the yearly salary cost of unauthorised teacher absence in India?
recall.a: $1.5 billion.

recall.q: Why do simple performance pay schemes often disappoint in government?
recall.a: Agencies face several principals, multitasking, hard-to-measure output and weak exit.

sections.title: Corruption and how to measure it
sections.big_idea: Measure corruption **directly, by comparing records with reality**, because perception indices cannot locate leakage.
in_plain_words: Corruption takes several forms: petty bribes, grand kickbacks, leakage and capture. Coercive and collusive bribes need different remedies. Indian law is narrower and more specific than the working definition. The 2018 amendment made bribe giving an offence in its own right, and section 17A on prior approval is under reconsideration after a split verdict.

Perception indices such as the Corruption Perceptions Index are slow to move and cannot locate the problem. Experience surveys name the service and who paid, and direct methods such as engineering audits, beneficiary verification and phone checks find leakage. Map **prevent, detect, sanction and protect** for your service before adding another tool.

diagram.caption: a district with one function missing is thin

key_terms.meaning: A bribe for a certificate, ration card or land record.
Fake names on muster rolls, diverted grain, ghost pensioners.
Transparency International's perception index, 0 to 100.
Prior approval before inquiry into official decisions.
Independent estimate of materials compared with reported spending.

worked_example.title: What an audit can change
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. Olken raised the audit chance on village roads from 4% to 100% and cut missing spending by eight points. Suppose a similar programme starts at 24% missing.
steps: The audit chance rose by 100 − 4 = 96 percentage points.
Missing expenditure falls by eight points, so 24 − 8 = 16 per cent of spending is still missing.
Grassroots monitoring alone had little average effect in the same study, so the audit is the active ingredient.
worked_example.answer: Missing spending falls from 24% to 16% in this illustration. A direct measure is what shows the change.

mistakes: Treating perception scores as a map of where leakage occurs.
Using one remedy for both coercive and collusive bribes.
Relying on s17A without checking the current position after the January 2026 split verdict.
Adding a new detection tool where detection already exists but sanctions do not.

recall.q: What share of public service users in India reported paying a bribe in the Global Corruption Barometer Asia 2020?
recall.a: 39 percent, the highest in the survey.

recall.q: Name three direct measures of corruption.
recall.a: Any three of: engineering audit, random public audits, beneficiary verification, unannounced visits, phone checks.

recall.q: What did the 2018 amendment change about bribe giving?
recall.a: It made bribe giving an offence in its own right and made commercial organisations liable.

recall.q: Which Indian instrument is listed under Protect?
recall.a: The Whistle Blowers Protection Act 2014, which is not operational.

sections.title: Decentralisation: funds, functions, functionaries
sections.big_idea: Devolution is real only when a local body has **functions, funds and functionaries**, and guards against capture.
in_plain_words: The 73rd and 74th Amendments gave constitutional status to panchayats and municipalities, with reservations for SCs, STs and women and State Finance Commissions every fifth year. The key word in Articles 243G and 243W is 'may': states decide which subjects, how much money and which staff, so devolution varies widely.

RBI data show that over 95 percent of panchayat revenue is grants-in-aid and only about 1.1 percent comes from own taxes. Kerala's People's Plan shows deep devolution with rules about spending. Elite capture is the risk, so look for the signs and use counterweights. **Check all three Fs before giving a panchayat a role.**

diagram.note: strong on one F and weak on the others is still a weak partner

key_terms.meaning: Inserted Part IX on panchayats; in force from 24 April 1993.
Inserted Part IXA on municipalities.
Constituted every fifth year under Article 243I.
Local power passing to dominant castes, landlords or contractors.
Money a panchayat can spend as it decides.

worked_example.title: Where does a panchayat's money come from?
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a panchayat has revenue receipts of Rs 100 lakh. Use the RBI shares from the deck, over 95% from grants-in-aid and 1.1% from own taxes.
steps: Grants-in-aid are at least 100 × 0.95 = 95 lakh.
Own taxes: 100 × 0.011 = 1.1 lakh.
The rest of the receipts at most: 100 − 95 − 1.1 = 3.9 lakh.
With so little local money, voters who pay little locally may demand little locally.
worked_example.answer: At least Rs 95 lakh from grants, Rs 1.1 lakh from own taxes and at most Rs 3.9 lakh from everything else.

mistakes: Assuming a gram panchayat controls a function without reading the state's Panchayati Raj Act and devolution orders.
Judging devolution on funds alone and ignoring who appoints the staff.
Accepting a gram sabha held on paper, with identical signatures, as participation.
Treating all of India as Kerala. Devolution depends on each state.

recall.q: What does Article 243D provide?
recall.a: Reservation for SCs and STs in proportion to population and at least one-third of seats for women.

recall.q: What does the Eleventh Schedule list?
recall.a: 29 subjects that panchayats may be given.

recall.q: What share of panchayat revenue comes from own taxes?
recall.a: About 1.1 percent in 2020 to 2022, and 1.0 percent in 2022 to 2023.

recall.q: Name two signs of elite capture.
recall.a: Any two of: identical signatures on gram sabha minutes, works in one hamlet, beneficiary lists tracking one family's network, reserved members silent.

sections.title: Transparency and the RTI Act
sections.big_idea: RTI is a demand-side right and a supply-side duty, but its strength now rests on **time limits, exemptions and weak commissions**.
in_plain_words: Any citizen can request information from a public authority without giving a reason (s6), and authorities must publish key information themselves (s4(1)(b)). A request moves from the PIO to a first appeal and a second appeal, each with a deadline. Silence after 30 days is a deemed refusal, and a penalty can fall on the PIO.

Section 8 lets authorities withhold information, but s8(2) allows disclosure when the public interest outweighs the harm. The 2019 amendment gave the central government control of commissioners' terms and pay, and the DPDP Act substituted a much shorter clause (j) from 13 November 2025. Commissions are the bottleneck, with 4,13,972 appeals pending. **Frame requests around public functions and aggregate data.**

events.what: Reply if life or liberty is involved
Reply due; silence is deemed refusal
Second appeal to CIC or SIC (s19(3))

diagram.caption: the RTI sequence, with the deadline at every step

key_terms.meaning: Public Information Officer who receives and answers requests.
No reply within the time counts as refusal under s7(2).
Public interest override for exempt information.
Exemption for personal information; rewritten in 2025.
Publishing records without being asked under s4.

worked_example.title: Diarise a request and size the penalty
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: you file an RTI request on day 0. The deck says diarise day 30 for the reply and day 60 for the first appeal. The penalty is Rs 250 a day up to Rs 25,000.
steps: Reply due on day 30.
First appeal must be filed within 30 days of that: 30 + 30 = 60, which is the day to diarise.
Penalty per day of delay: Rs 250, capped at Rs 25,000.
The cap is reached after 25,000 ÷ 250 = 100 days of delay.
worked_example.answer: Diarise day 30 and day 60. The maximum penalty on the PIO is reached after 100 days.

mistakes: Asking questions or opinions in an RTI request instead of asking for records.
Accepting a bare s8 citation as a refusal without appealing.
Missing the 30-day deadline for the first appeal and ending the case.
Citing the 2005 text of clause (j) without noting the 2025 substitution.

recall.q: How long does a PIO have to reply, and what if life or liberty is involved?
recall.a: 30 days, or 48 hours if life or liberty is involved.

recall.q: What is the penalty under s20?
recall.a: Rs 250 a day on the PIO, up to Rs 25,000.

recall.q: What did section 44(3) of the DPDP Act do to the RTI Act?
recall.a: It substituted a new clause (j) in s8(1) that exempts information relating to personal information, in force from 13 November 2025.

recall.q: What did the 2024 Constitution Bench decision strike down?
recall.a: The 2018 Electoral Bond Scheme, as violating voters' right to information.

sections.title: Social audit and citizen monitoring
sections.big_idea: A social audit is **public verification of records by the people the programme serves**, and it works when someone acts on the findings.
in_plain_words: Records are collected, checked door to door against what workers and residents say, and read out at a public hearing where officials must answer. The method grew from MKSS public hearings in Rajasthan into a statutory duty under MGNREGA, and now rests on s20 of the VB-G RAM G Act 2025 and rules made under s33.

Trials of community monitoring give mixed results. Information alone rarely moves providers, while a forum, a clear standard and a route to consequences help. Protect people who speak up from retaliation. **Plan the follow-up before you plan the hearing**, or the audit becomes a ritual that produces reports and disillusion.

nodes.label: Verification
nodes.sub: door to door, at work sites

diagram.caption: the loop closes only if action is tracked into the next round

key_terms.meaning: Public verification of records against reality.
Public hearing where officials answer testimony.
User survey comparing providers or areas.
Users and providers score a facility and agree actions.
Following funds from budget to facility.

worked_example.title: Score a village against the checklist
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a gram panchayat meets five of the deck's eight conditions (records, known standards, independent team, forum, timely action) and lacks protection, published findings and marginalised voices.
steps: Count the conditions present: records, standards, independent team, forum and action: 5.
Count the gaps: 8 − 5 = 3.
The missing items are protection from retaliation, published and tracked findings, and marginalised groups speaking alongside the village elite.
Fix the protection gap first, since people who testify can face threats.
worked_example.answer: Five of eight present, three gaps. Start with protecting complainants.

mistakes: Holding a hearing with no one authorised to act on the findings.
Running the audit with a team that depends on the implementing agency.
Assuming information alone will move providers.
Naming complainants in published findings without their agreement.

recall.q: What are the four steps of a social audit?
recall.a: Records, verification, public hearing and action taken.

recall.q: What did Bjorkman and Svensson find in Uganda?
recall.a: Community monitoring led to more effort by health workers, higher use and lower child mortality.

recall.q: Which section of the VB-G RAM G Act sets the Gram Sabha's social audit duty?
recall.a: Section 20.

recall.q: Name two protective practices from the deck.
recall.a: Any two of: file requests through organisations, aggregate testimony, brief district officials first, keep a referral route to legal aid.

sections.title: Grievances, charters and the Lokpal
sections.big_idea: A grievance system fixes cases, and it becomes an accountability tool only when **complaints are analysed and acted on**.
in_plain_words: A citizen charter promises standards but has no legal force, while a right to service law makes delivery within a notified time a duty with penalties. CPGRAMS, the central grievance portal, reports faster disposal, but 'disposed' means closed by the department and not resolved for the citizen. Match each problem to the right channel and keep copies and dates.

The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act 2013 took more than five years to produce a Lokpal, and the Whistle Blowers Protection Act 2014 has no commencement date. **Creating an agency in law does not create it in fact.** Inside your own programme, run confidential channels and keep the person who reports apart from the person who investigates.

diagram.caption: five routes with very different strength

key_terms.meaning: A statement of service standards without legal force.
A law making timely delivery a legal duty.
Centralised Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System.
State-level anti-corruption body under s63 of the 2013 Act.
2004 resolution under which the CVC receives disclosures.

worked_example.title: Read the CPGRAMS numbers
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's official figures: 27 lakh grievances in 2024 against about 3.01 lakh in 2014, 15 days average disposal in 2025 against 157 in 2014.
steps: Volume rose by 27 ÷ 3.01 = 8.97, about nine times.
Disposal time fell by 157 ÷ 15 = 10.5, about ten times faster.
Faster closure is a process figure. 'Disposed' means closed by the department.
To use CPGRAMS as accountability, group complaints by office, scheme and cause, and test whether the same office keeps appearing.
worked_example.answer: Volume is about nine times higher and closure about ten times faster. Satisfaction and patterns still need your own record.

mistakes: Treating a charter as an enforceable right.
Closing a grievance by forwarding it or replying without action, then counting it as resolved.
Relying on the Whistle Blowers Protection Act 2014 before checking the Gazette for its status.
Sending every problem to the same office instead of choosing the right channel.

recall.q: Which state enacted the first right to service law, and when?
recall.a: Madhya Pradesh, on 18 August 2010.

recall.q: When did the first Lokpal take office?
recall.a: 23 March 2019, which was P.C. Ghose.

recall.q: What must each state do under s63 of the Lokpal Act?
recall.a: Establish a Lokayukta by state law within one year of commencement, if not already established.

recall.q: What should you do first when information is refused?
recall.a: File a first appeal under s19(1) of the RTI Act.

sections.title: Audit institutions, e-governance and DBT
sections.big_idea: Audits, payment reform and phone checks can cut leakage, but each brings a trade-off to watch, especially **exclusion**.
in_plain_words: The CAG is protected by a removal process like a Supreme Court judge's and by reports that go to the legislature. Audit becomes accountability when the Public Accounts Committee examines the report and the department answers. Experiments show that audits reduce missing expenditure, and that publishing results can change elections.

Direct Benefit Transfer pays benefits into bank accounts. Smartcards and e-invoicing cut leakage at scale, and phone monitoring reduced unpaid transfers cheaply. Stricter biometric checks excluded 1.5 to 2 million legitimate beneficiaries at some point. **Track exclusion as carefully as leakage**, and use dashboards as the start of field checks.

key_terms.meaning: Comptroller and Auditor-General, India's supreme audit institution.
Legislative committee that examines CAG reports.
Asks whether a programme achieved its aims.
Direct Benefit Transfer into bank accounts.
Biometric payment system tested in Andhra Pradesh.

worked_example.title: Read the DBT and phone-call numbers
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's figures: beneficiaries rose from 11 crore to 176 crore, subsidies fell from 16% to 9% of expenditure, and phone monitoring cost 3.6 cents per additional dollar delivered.
steps: Beneficiary coverage grew by 176 ÷ 11 = 16 times.
The subsidy share fell by 16 − 9 = 7 percentage points.
Phone monitoring that delivers an extra $10,000 costs about 10,000 × 0.036 = 360 dollars.
Check exclusion: count who was removed and sample the removed names at the door.
worked_example.answer: Coverage is 16 times higher, the subsidy share is 7 points lower, and an extra $10,000 delivered costs about $360.

mistakes: Quoting 'savings' without asking how many were eligible people wrongly removed.
Reading a CAG finding as a consequence. It needs the committee and the department to act.
Treating a dashboard as proof that a recorded worker was the real worker.
Expecting technology to help citizens who cannot read the dashboard.

recall.q: What protects the CAG's independence?
recall.a: Removal only like a Supreme Court judge, and reports routed to the legislature.

recall.q: What did Ferraz and Finan find?
recall.a: Releasing audit results before the 2004 elections affected incumbents' performance, more where local radio spread the news.

recall.q: What did Muralidharan, Niehaus and Sukhtankar find about stricter biometric checks?
recall.a: Corruption fell, but 1.5 to 2 million legitimate beneficiaries lost access at some point.

recall.q: What does section 24 of the VB-G RAM G Act require?
recall.a: Biometric authentication, geospatial planning, dashboards and weekly disclosure of muster rolls, payments and grievances.

sections.title: Putting it to work: a practitioner's toolkit
sections.big_idea: Run a **ten-question diagnostic** first, then pick the tool that fits the weak link and measure it.
in_plain_words: The diagnostic takes a few days of document review and interviews and covers the entitlement, the provider, funds and functionaries, records, the weakest WDR relationship, grievance routes, who benefits from the failure, who is excluded and what frontline workers say. The decision table then matches diagnosis to tool and evidence.

Good RTI requests ask for records and leave opinions out. Governance indicators for your MEL framework are concrete, such as presence on visits and receipt confirmed by phone. Protect personal data when collecting and publishing, and keep independence when you work with officials. **Pilot with measurement** before scaling any tool.

diagram.caption: the ration-shop example from the deck

key_terms.meaning: Ten questions to find the weak link before choosing a tool.
An RTI request asking for opinions or conclusions.
A request for specific records, a place and a period.
Publish entitlements, open records, two-way channel, independent check.
DPDP research exemption that excludes decisions on named individuals.

worked_example.title: Measure the ration-shop pilot
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: the NGO surveys 100 cardholders before and after the pilot. In round one, 38 confirm they received the full entitlement. In round two, 61 do.
steps: Round one share: 38 of 100 is 38%.
Round two share: 61 of 100 is 61%.
Change: 61 − 38 = 23 percentage points.
Check what to watch: retaliation against families who testified, and grievances closed without action.
worked_example.answer: Verified receipt rose by 23 points, which is the kind of evidence the deck says success looks like.

mistakes: Applying a favourite tool before running the diagnostic.
Asking an RTI question like 'who is responsible for the corruption?'
Publishing names from a beneficiary list without consent or a clear public interest.
Taking funding from the department you audit for the same activity.

recall.q: What does a strong RTI request ask for?
recall.a: Specific records, such as sanction orders and payment vouchers, for a named place and period.

recall.q: Name two governance indicators for an MEL framework.
recall.a: Any two of: share of visits with provider present, beneficiaries confirming receipt, disclosures displayed, women and SC/ST speaking share, days to resolve grievances, findings with action.

recall.q: What are the four programme commitments?
recall.a: Publish entitlements, open records, a two-way channel and an independent check.

recall.q: What should you do before going public with findings?
recall.a: Present them to officials first.

sections.title: State capacity, evidence and where next
sections.big_idea: The Indian state both fails and succeeds, and the way out is **building and sequencing capacity** from local problems.
in_plain_words: Pritchett described India's state as flailing: a capable head in the central ministries and elite services no longer reliably connected to the arms and legs of implementation. Pritchett, Woolcock and Andrews name isomorphic mimicry and premature load bearing, and propose Problem-Driven Iterative Adaptation as a way out. Kapur finds the state does better on episodic tasks than on daily delivery.

The evidence summary is cautious. Monitoring with consequences, payment technology and organised community monitoring show gains, each with a caveat. Use the patterns as hypotheses and test them. **Ask of any new commission, portal or law: who will run it, with what staff, and what happens when the load arrives?**

left.title: The capability trap
items: Isomorphic mimicry hides a lack of function

right.title: A way out: PDIA
items: Start from a named local problem

key_terms.meaning: Strong head, weak connection to implementation.
Adopting forms while function stays absent.
Demands placed on systems faster than capability grows.
Problem-Driven Iterative Adaptation.
A task with a built-in end, such as an election.

worked_example.title: Classify three reforms
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: apply the deck's three concepts to a district proposal.
steps: A new grievance portal is launched with no staff to answer it. The form exists and the function does not, so this is isomorphic mimicry.
A state asks a weak department to run five new schemes in a year. Demands outpace capability, so this is premature load bearing.
A district picks one named delivery problem, tests a fix, checks results every month and adapts. This follows PDIA.
The test for each: who will run it, with what staff, and what happens when the load arrives?
worked_example.answer: Mimicry, premature load bearing and PDIA respectively.

mistakes: Believing more schemes and more money fix a flailing state.
Treating the evidence table as universal laws instead of hypotheses to test.
Confusing existence of an agency on paper with its capacity to work.
Skipping Impact Evaluation 101 before designing a test of a governance intervention.

recall.q: What did Pritchett mean by a flailing state?
recall.a: A capable head not reliably connected to the arms and legs of implementation.

recall.q: What does Kapur say about episodic tasks?
recall.a: The Indian state does better on episodic tasks with an end, such as elections and vaccination drives, than on daily delivery.

recall.q: What is the core claim of Muralidharan's 2024 book?
recall.a: Quality public services turn the political equality of one person, one vote into greater equality of opportunity.

recall.q: Which finding is supported by Ferraz and Finan 2008?
recall.a: Publishing audits changes elections, and needs media reach.

notes.2: Use the agenda as a reading order. Sections 2 and 3 give the theory, 4 to 9 give the law and the tools, and 10 and 11 turn them into practice. If you only run programmes, **read section 10 first** and use the earlier sections as reference.
notes.4: The two schools in the slide give you a quick question to ask of any programme. Skip the question of whether the inputs exist and ask **who decides, who delivers, who checks and what happens when delivery fails**. That is the governance view the whole course uses.
notes.5: Memorise the definition and then the contrast: government is the set of organisations, governance is how those organisations plus citizens, parties, media and markets behave together. **A large government can have weak governance**, and a small one can work well.
notes.6: Learn the six WGI dimensions as a list: voice and accountability, political stability, government effectiveness, regulatory quality, rule of law, control of corruption. Notice that each is a composite of many survey and expert questions, so it summarises **perceptions** and does not count outputs.
notes.7: Hold three numbers: 35 sources, over 400 questions, and 1996 to 2025. The World Bank's own advisory is the sentence to quote when someone treats a score as a verdict. These are **estimates based on perceptions** that can lag behind reforms.
notes.8: Use the four cautions as questions to ask of any index: whose perception, how stale, how aggregated, how uncertain. The practical rule at the bottom matters most. **Never justify a decision about a single programme site with a national score.**
notes.9: The good-governance agenda taught two lessons. Institutions matter, and copying forms does not copy results. Remember the term **isomorphic mimicry**: adopting the forms of functional states while the function stays absent. Judge an institution by what it does in your district.
notes.10: The table gives you five dates to anchor the region: RTI laws in India 2005, Nepal 2007, Bangladesh 2009, Sri Lanka 2016 and Pakistan 2017. The text points to the key idea: **the gap between what the law promises and what a citizen receives** is where governance lives.
notes.12: Split every accountability tool into two questions: does it produce information (answerability), and can anyone impose a consequence (enforcement)? Explanation without sanction is public relations. **Test each tool on both halves** before you rely on it.
notes.13: Put examples in each box. Vertical: elections and a free press, which are periodic and blunt. Horizontal: CAG, courts, Lokpal and commissions, which are continuous but depend on independence. O'Donnell's last point links them: **public opinion is what pushes agencies to act**.
notes.14: Societal or diagonal accountability is where most development programmes sit. The MKSS hearings are the Indian model. Use the table to ask which lever your project pulls. If it only mobilises citizens, **it works through the third direction**, and still needs horizontal agencies to respond.
notes.15: Learn the four relationships by the arrows between the three corners: voice, compact, management and client power. Each has a PHC example in the table. The triangle's value is that it tells you **which relationship to repair** before you choose a tool.
notes.16: Contrast the two routes in a sentence. The long route runs citizen to politician to department to provider and breaks when votes turn on caste or handouts. The short route gives citizens power over providers directly. The Bangladesh school example shows **paying schools by girls enrolled**.
notes.17: Treat the 74 percent as a lesson about the gap between posts filled and services delivered, since the deck itself says the survey is old. Read the closing contrast carefully: absence tells you two relationships are failing and **does not tell you the fix**.
notes.18: Work through the four questions for a service you know. In the anganwadi example, one failure has four possible breaks and each points to a different remedy. The bottom line is the point: **fixing the wrong relationship wastes the programme's effort**.
notes.20: Fix the model in your head: a principal hires an agent who knows more about their own effort. Use the two examples to tell the problems apart. Home visits that never happened are hidden action. A contractor's cost estimate is hidden information. **Monitoring, incentives and selection** are the three responses.
notes.21: Draw the chain from citizens to the frontline worker and mark where information is lost. A complaint about a ration shop becomes one line in a monthly report by the time it reaches the state. **Shorter chains help**, which is the case for decentralisation and the short route.
notes.22: Use the table to explain why simple performance pay disappoints in government. Several principals, multitasking, hard-to-measure output and weak exit each undermine it. The closing rule is practical: **check that the measured task is the one that matters**.
notes.23: Record the three headline figures: 19 percent of teachers and 35 percent of health workers absent across six countries, and in India about half of teachers actually teaching. The closing line is the lesson. **Presence is only the floor**, and effort needs its own measure.
notes.24: Note the comparison: inputs improved but absence fell only modestly. The $1.5 billion yearly cost of unauthorised absence and the finding that monitoring is more than ten times as cost-effective as hiring teachers lead to the policy point. **Weak management makes input spending buy less.**
notes.25: Sort every tool in this course into monitoring, incentives, selection, or voice and exit, then note the failure the slide attaches to each. The closing line is the practical rule. **Combine monitoring with consequences that someone actually applies.**
notes.26: Read this slide before you criticise frontline staff. Election duty, long travel, unpaid salaries and rules that reward paperwork explain absence as well as laziness. Diagnose the system before you choose sanctions, and **talk to frontline workers early**, since they know where the chain breaks above them.
notes.28: Use the four forms to classify any case you hear about: petty, grand, leakage or capture. The final distinction is the one to remember. Coercive bribes (pay or be refused a right) and collusive bribes (pay to break a rule) **need different remedies**.
notes.29: Follow the three legal points: bribe giving became an offence in its own right in 2018, companies are liable for bribes given on their behalf, and section 17A requires prior approval for some inquiries. The Court split in January 2026, so **check the current position before relying on 17A**.
notes.30: Read the ranks out of 182 as a spread: Bhutan 18, India 91, Sri Lanka 107, Nepal 109, Pakistan 136, Bangladesh 150. The scale runs from 0 (highly corrupt) to 100 (very clean). It is perception data, so use it for **long-run cross-country patterns**.
notes.31: Contrast experts with citizens. The Barometer asked nearly 20,000 people in 17 countries what they paid. In India 39 percent of public service users reported paying a bribe. Experience data are closer to action because they **name the service, the frequency and who paid**.
notes.32: Use the two columns to decide what question each type of measure can answer. A perception index suits long-run comparison across countries. Direct measurement locates leakage and tests a reform. The slide ends on the instruction: **measure delivery**.
notes.33: Treat the five methods as a toolkit you can adapt. Each compares a record with reality: engineers against reported spending, audits against voters, lists against real beneficiaries, visits against presence, calls against receipt. **A small version of each is within reach of an MEL team.**
notes.34: Use the four functions to map the system for your service. A district with detection and no sanction produces audit paragraphs and no change. A district with harsh sanctions and no detection punishes only the unlucky. **Map which of the four functions exist before adding a tool.**
notes.36: List the arguments on each side before you take a position. Decentralisation brings better information and a shorter chain, but it can meet thin capacity and elite capture. The slide's last line is the reading to adopt: **design and finance decide which side wins**.
notes.37: Learn the structure by pairs: Article 243G and 243W for powers, the Eleventh Schedule's 29 subjects and the Twelfth Schedule's 18 functions, and 243I and 243Y for finance commissions. Reservation sits in 243D and 243T. The 73rd Amendment came into force on **24 April 1993**.
notes.38: The word 'may' is the key to the slide. The Constitution guarantees terms, elections, reserved seats and finance commissions, but **leaves devolution of subjects, money and staff to each state**. Before assuming a gram panchayat controls a function, read your state's Act and devolution orders.
notes.39: Remember the rule and the evidence. Article 243D reserves at least one-third of directly elected seats for women, including within the SC and ST quotas. The Chattopadhyay and Duflo study is strong because **posts were randomly reserved**. Watch for proxy rule by male relatives.
notes.40: Assess any panchayat on all three Fs before giving it a role. Ask the question in the middle column for each, then look for the warning sign. A panchayat that is strong on one F and weak on the others **is still a weak partner** for accountability work.
notes.41: Keep the three RBI numbers in mind: over 95 percent of revenue is grants-in-aid, about 1.1 percent comes from own taxes, and about 80 percent is Central grants alone. The last sentence draws the lesson. **Voters who pay little locally may demand little locally.**
notes.42: Use this slide to find where local body money comes from. Article 243I sets up a State Finance Commission every fifth year, and the Union Finance Commission also gives grants. The Fifteenth Finance Commission total for 2021 to 2026 was **Rs 4,36,361 crore**.
notes.43: Study Kerala for its design rules as well as its scale. The state devolved 35 to 40 percent of plan funds from 1996, set a quorum of ten percent for ward grama sabhas, and attached conditions on how funds were used. **Deep devolution came with rules about spending.**
notes.44: Compare the three constitutional routes. India's devolution varies by state. Nepal created 753 local levels under the 2015 Constitution. Pakistan's Article 140A requires each province to set up a local system. The practitioner note is the useful one: **check the state or provincial law**.
notes.45: Use the two columns as a field checklist. Identical signatures on gram sabha minutes, works concentrated in one hamlet and silent reserved members are signs of capture. The counterweights, such as **public reading of beneficiary lists**, cost little to introduce.
notes.47: The RTI Act has a demand side and a supply side. Any citizen can request without giving a reason (s6), and every authority must publish information on its own initiative (s4(1)(b)). Section 2(h) matters for you: **an NGO substantially financed by government may be a public authority**.
notes.48: Do not memorise the table. Learn four anchors: s6 to make a request, s7 for the 30-day deadline, s8 for the exemptions, and s19 for appeals. Then add s20, the penalty of **Rs 250 a day up to Rs 25,000** on the PIO. Return to the rest when you need them.
notes.49: Follow the sequence and attach a time limit to each step: reply in 30 days, first appeal in 30 days, second appeal in 90 days. Silence after 30 days is a **deemed refusal** and you can appeal at once. If life or liberty is at stake, the reply is due in 48 hours.
notes.50: When a refusal arrives, check whether it names the section and explains why it applies. A bare citation of s8 is a ground for first appeal. Keep section 8(2), the public interest override, ready, since it was **not changed by the 2023 amendment**.
notes.51: Compare before and after: a fixed five-year term and pay linked to the Election Commission became a three-year term set by the central government. The slide's conclusion is the one to repeat. **Horizontal accountability depends on independence**, and executive-set terms change incentives.
notes.52: Read the two versions of clause (j) next to each other. The 2005 text had a public activity test and a larger public interest test. The substituted clause says only that the information 'relates to personal information'. Section 44(3) took effect on **13 November 2025**.
notes.53: The practical effect is that many requests about officials, lists and payments can now be refused with s8(1)(j) alone. Use the three arguments in the table and note their status. Frame requests around **public functions and aggregate data**, and cite s8(2) and the disclosure duties.
notes.54: Memorise the pending figure: 4,13,972 appeals and complaints on 30 June 2025 across 29 commissions. Then note the delay and vacancy facts. The slide's opening sentence is the thesis: **a right is only as good as the body that enforces it**.
notes.55: Learn the two cases as pairs of year, court and holding. In 2019 the Chief Justice's office was held to be a public authority under s2(h). In 2024 the Electoral Bond Scheme was struck down as violating voters' right to information. Both show **courts widening access to information about public power**.
notes.56: Read the scores as a rating of the text of the law, out of 150. India's 126 uses the 2005 Act without the 2019 and 2023 amendments. The warning at the bottom is the important one: **a strong law and a slow commission can coexist**.
notes.58: Learn the four steps: records, verification, public hearing, action taken. The unique feature is that **the people named in the records confirm or deny them**, so ghost workers surface. Without independent resource persons and officials who must act, the process fails.
notes.59: Trace the line from MKSS jan sunwais to a statutory duty under Section 17 of MGNREGA 2005. Andhra Pradesh built the first large system. Its lesson is double: commitment and a dedicated office matter, and **audits uncover problems faster than departments act**.
notes.60: Use the table as a map of where social audit now sits: s20 for the Gram Sabha's duty and the records to be provided, s18(5)(d) for the Programme Officer, s24 for weekly disclosure, and s33 for rules. **Check the rules before designing audit work.**
notes.61: Compare the two Acts. Both place social audit on the Gram Sabha. The new Act adds technology-based monitoring and weekly disclosure, and rules now come from the Centre under s33. Whether audits stay **independent of the implementing agency** depends on those rules.
notes.62: Memorise the pattern across the three trials. Meetings run by an NGO in Uganda improved outcomes. Information alone in Uttar Pradesh did not change involvement, though volunteer reading camps raised reading. In Indonesia, audits cut missing spending by eight points. **Information needs a forum, a standard and a consequence.**
notes.63: Choose the tool by the job. Citizen report cards compare, scorecards solve problems at one facility, social audits detect leakage, expenditure tracking follows money, and hearings press specific cases. The table also points to **Participatory Methods 101 and Advocacy Basics 101** for next steps.
notes.64: Run this eight-point list before investing in a social accountability component. None of the conditions is enough alone. The last sentence sets the plan: **design follow-up before you design the hearing**, because an audit without action becomes a ritual.
notes.65: Treat protection as part of the design. RTI users and audit resource persons have faced threats and violence. The protective practices on the slide are concrete: file through organisations, aggregate testimony, brief district officials before the hearing, and keep a **referral route to legal aid**.
notes.67: Distinguish the charter from the law. A citizen charter promises standards but has no legal force. A right to service law makes delivery within a notified time a duty and allows penalties. Madhya Pradesh enacted the first on 18 August 2010. **Check your state's notified list.**
notes.68: Read the three numbers as official progress: 27 lakh grievances in 2024, 15 days average disposal in 2025, and over 1.11 lakh grievance officers. The final line is the caution. **'Disposed' means closed by the department**, which is different from resolved to the citizen's satisfaction.
notes.69: Separate fixing a case from changing behaviour. Grievance redress closes one complaint at a time and is measured by disposal time. It becomes an accountability tool when complaints are grouped by office and cause. **Keep copies of complaints and replies** as your evidence.
notes.70: Remember the Lokpal's structure: a Chairperson and up to eight Members, half judicial, with representation of SCs, STs, OBCs, minorities and women. It has jurisdiction over the Prime Minister with exclusions. Section 63 requires each state to set up a **Lokayukta** within one year.
notes.71: Follow the five dates: assent on 1 January 2014, the first Lokpal on 23 March 2019, the acting arrangement from 2022, and a Chairperson from 10 March 2024. The lesson is blunt. **Creating an agency in law does not create it in fact.**
notes.72: The Whistle Blowers Protection Act 2014 was published but no date for it to come into force has been notified. Insiders therefore depend on service rules and goodwill. Inside your own programme, run a **confidential channel and separate the person who reports from the person who investigates**.
notes.73: Use the table to route each problem to its first channel and its fallback. Information refused goes to s19 appeals, rural works to social audit under s20, bribes to the anti-corruption bureau or police. The instruction at the bottom is practical: **keep copies and dates of everything**.
notes.75: Learn the four articles in order: 148 for appointment and removal, 149 for duties, 150 for the form of accounts, and 151 for reports to the President or Governor. The CAG's **independence comes from removal like a Supreme Court judge** and reports routed to the legislature.
notes.76: Trace the path from audit to consequence and mark where it can stall. The Public Accounts Committee is the main link in India. Remember the two types: compliance audit checks rules and performance audit checks results. **CAG performance audits are free, rigorous evaluations**, so read them before you design a baseline.
notes.77: Pair the two studies. Olken raised audit probability from 4 to 100 percent and cut missing spending by eight points. Ferraz and Finan published audits before elections and found an effect on incumbents. The conclusion: **top-down audit works, and works better when citizens see the results**.
notes.78: Read the DBT figures as the government's case: Rs 3.48 lakh crore in attributed savings, subsidies falling from 16 to 9 percent of expenditure, beneficiaries rising from 11 crore to 176 crore. The caution is the key skill. **'Savings' can include eligible people wrongly removed.**
notes.79: Note the trade-off both studies report. Smartcards in Andhra Pradesh made payments faster and less corrupt without cutting access. Just-in-time payments cut spending by 24 percent but raised delays. **Technology can tighten control while adding friction** for workers.
notes.80: Keep the exclusion figure in view: 1.5 to 2 million legitimate beneficiaries lost access at some point during the reforms. The authors say the harm came mainly from how the transition was managed. For your own work, **track exclusion as carefully as leakage**.
notes.81: The phone-call study shows monitoring without inspectors. Officials knew beneficiaries would be called, and the share of farmers not receiving their transfers fell 7.8 percent at 3.6 cents per additional dollar delivered. **Adapt it by calling a random sample monthly** and sharing results with district officials.
notes.82: Technology records and reports, and it cannot verify. Section 24 of the VB-G RAM G Act lists biometric authentication, geospatial planning and weekly disclosure. A recorded worker may not be the real worker. Use dashboards **as a starting point for field checks** and print key figures for the gram sabha.
notes.84: Run the ten questions before choosing a tool. They take a few days of document review and interviews. Two deserve extra attention: who benefits from the current failure, and what a frontline worker says is the real constraint. **Write the answers on one page** and share it.
notes.85: Treat the table as a starting point that matches a diagnosis to a tool and a study to read. For example, absent providers point to unannounced visits, and eligible people removed from lists point to an exclusion audit. **A pilot with measurement** tells you whether it works in your district.
notes.86: Follow the ration-shop sequence: RTI for registers, a survey of 100 cardholders, a gram sabha hearing, tracked grievances, and a pattern shared with the district supply officer. The 'what to watch' box is as important as the plan. **Retaliation and closed-without-action grievances** are the risks.
notes.87: Compare the weak and strong requests. A weak one asks for opinions and conclusions. A strong one asks for specific records, a place and a period. Diarise day 30 for the reply and day 60 for the first appeal, and **ask for aggregate data** given the new s8(1)(j).
notes.88: Apply the four commitments to your own organisation: publish entitlements, open records, run a two-way channel and allow an independent check. Each has a test in the right-hand column. The last line explains why: **you ask government for these standards, so apply them to yourself**.
notes.89: Choose a few indicators for your MEL framework, one from each level if possible. They are concrete and observable: presence on visits, receipt confirmed by phone, disclosures displayed, women and SC/ST speaking share, days to resolve grievances, and findings acted on. **None needs a national index.**
notes.90: Plan data protection before you start collecting. Decide the minimum data needed, get informed consent, aggregate before publishing, and delete when no longer needed. The research exemption in s17(2)(b) **does not cover monitoring that acts on named cases**, so treat those with the full duties.
notes.91: Both risks are real: ambush if you surprise officials, and co-option if you depend on the department you monitor. The actions on the slide manage both. Share plans early, present findings to officials first, and **do not take funding from the department you audit** for the same activity.
notes.93: Pritchett's image is a capable head not connected to the arms and legs of implementation. It explains why good laws produce poor services. The implication is the useful part. **More schemes and money do not fix a flailing state**, because capacity must be built, measured and protected.
notes.94: Learn the three terms: isomorphic mimicry hides a lack of function, premature load bearing demands more than capacity allows, and PDIA solves named local problems by trying and adapting. Ask of any new portal or commission: **who will run it, with what staff, and what happens when the load arrives?**
notes.95: Kapur's pattern is a good question to ask of any scheme: is it an episodic task with an end, like an election or a vaccination drive, or daily delivery? The state does better on the first. He questions two myths: that the state is bloated and that it is submerged in patronage.
notes.96: Muralidharan's book builds a state-led reform roadmap from many studies in this course. The core claim links services to equality: quality public services turn one person, one vote into greater equality of opportunity. Treat it as a **bridge from the evidence to state-level reform design**.
notes.97: Use this as a set of hypotheses to test, since none is a universal law. Each finding has a caveat in the last column: the monitor must be independent, payment technology can delay or exclude, information needs a forum. Before testing a governance intervention yourself, **read Impact Evaluation 101**.
notes.98: Check yourself against the ten points. Each connects to a design choice, a legal duty or a measurement decision. The final line is the one that matters for law: **facts are stated as of October 2026**, so check for later amendments and judgments.
notes.99: Choose your next course by your gap. Indian Constitution 101 gives the legal foundations. Political Economy 101 explains the incentives behind capture. Public Finance and Budgeting 101 covers grants and fiscal federalism. Data Protection and the DPDP Act 101 covers personal data and RTI. **All courses are free.**
